label: flagship: wins all three exams
result: Final results, all solutions replay-checked. The flagship setting allows two ordinary moves before planning. Standard exam: 231 of 232 solved, with 0.94 extra moves vs perfect play. The old planning language cannot go below 1.17 extra moves, ever. This change broke that floor. With a third ordinary move allowed, the standard exam improves a little more, to 0.86 extra moves. Hard exam: 177 of 218 solved, with one to two fewer moves than every alternative. New boards: 188 of 200 solved, with 1.47 extra moves vs perfect. The win repeated with two different network pairs. It also worked, unchanged, on larger boards (17 wins, 0 losses on moves) and crowded boards (23 wins, 0 losses). One caution: the rival move-by-move planner here is the original network. A re-tuned version would likely close part of the measured gap (see the project log, entry 24).
conclusion: Our flagship planner and the biggest finding of the program. Letting the planner make one or two ordinary moves before subgoal planning beats every pure-subgoal planner, everywhere we tried. A third move adds only a little. The benefit stops there.
note: Search-only change (no training); stochasticity is the search rng only. Gates: unseen moves 31/1 p=1.5e-8; graded moves 30/0 p=1.9e-9.
